intro/hello: Welcome to C S two thirty one N: Convolutional Neural Networks for Visual Recognition.
intro/famous: First taught at Stanford in twenty fifteen, it became one of the most influential courses in machine learning.
intro/term: This companion follows the winter twenty sixteen run, taught by Fay-Fay Lee, Andrey Kar-pah-thee and Justin Johnson.
intro/roles: Kar-pah-thee wrote most of the notes, Johnson wrote the assignments, and the two gave most of the lectures.
intro/task: The course is about one problem above all: image classification. Look at a photo, and say what is in it.
intro/guess: A model turns the photo into ten scores, one per class, and guesses the class that scores highest.
intro/scratch: You build all of it from scratch, in plain num pie, before moving on to finding objects and captioning photos.
intro/site: This unofficial companion follows the same ideas in the same order, and builds each one up from first principles.
history/eyes: Lecture one starts far back, five hundred and forty million years ago, when the first eyes may have set off an explosion of animal life.
history/cat: In nineteen fifty nine, Hubel and Wiesel found cells in a cat's brain that fire for an edge at one angle.
history/blueprint: Simple detectors feeding more complex ones: the blueprint of a ConvNet.
history/features: For decades after, people designed image features by hand, and a simple classifier made the call.
history/imagenet: Then, in two thousand nine, came ImageNet: over fourteen million labeled photos, from Fay-Fay Lee's group.
history/contest: Its yearly contest gives a model five guesses per photo, and scores how often all five miss: the top-5 error.
history/early: Hand-designed pipelines won the first two years, with errors over twenty five percent.
history/alexnet: In twenty twelve, a ConvNet called Alex net cut the error to sixteen percent.
history/deeper: Every winner after that was a ConvNet, each deeper than the last.
history/resnet: By twenty fifteen, res net was at three point six percent, below one trained human's five point one.
history/fuel: The ideas were old. What changed was the fuel: big labeled datasets, fast graphics cards, and a few training tricks.
history/wave: C S two thirty one N was born in the middle of that wave, to teach these methods.
goal/end: By the end, you will have built an image classifier from the ground up, and understood every line.
goal/cifar: Most of the work uses see-far ten: tiny photos, thirty two pixels square, in ten classes.
goal/knn: You start with the simplest idea: label a photo by finding the most similar one you have already seen.
goal/lin: Then a linear classifier: one matrix multiply that scores every class at once.
goal/net: Then a neural network, trained with backpropagation: the chain rule, run backward through every layer.
goal/conv: Next, you split it into layers, each with a forward and a backward pass, and stack them into a ConvNet.
goal/rnn: Last come networks that caption photos, and tools for looking inside a trained network.
goal/three: Those are the three twenty sixteen assignments, and each one builds on the last.
map/five: Last, the map. The course has five parts.
map/start: Start here is this overview plus two toolkits, the math survival kit and Python with num pie, to come back to whenever you need.
map/nn: Neural networks is the core, best read in order: from the simplest classifier to backpropagation.
map/conv: Convolutional networks covers networks built for images: how they work, what they learn, and how they find objects.
map/beyond: Beyond still images adds sequences, attention, video, and learning without labels.
map/asg: And the three twenty sixteen assignments tie it all together, each one drawing on the chapters that teach it.
map/recap: That is the course: one problem, built from first principles, from a nearest neighbor to networks that caption photos.
map/next: Next, the math survival kit: the handful of ideas from calculus and linear algebra that everything else is built on.
